h: Rope Walk, the Riverside and Up Into Town
p: One of the nicest things about camping on Rope Walk is how little you need the car once you've arrived. The riverside meadows stretch out right by the Boat House, and the Wye Valley Walk, the long-distance trail that follows the river from Plynlimon down to Chepstow, passes through Ross, so you can head off on foot in either direction for as long or as short a ramble as your legs fancy.

Head upstream and you'll come to Wilton Bridge, a handsome 16th-century sandstone crossing that has spanned the Wye for over four hundred years. Walk the other way and climb the lanes into the town centre, where the red sandstone Market House sits on its pillars in the middle of the main square. It dates from the 17th century and is the obvious spot to get your bearings.

Just behind St Mary's Church you'll find The Prospect, a public garden laid out by John Kyrle, the local philanthropist remembered as the "Man of Ross". The view from the top over the great bend of the Wye and out to the Welsh hills is one of the best free treats in Herefordshire, and it's perfect for an evening wander after tea at the tent.

Goodrich Castle, a superb red sandstone ruin run by English Heritage, is a short drive south and is a real hit with kids who like spiral staircases and battlements. Carry on and you reach Symonds Yat for canoeing and that famous viewpoint, or cross into Wales for Monmouth. Hereford, with its cathedral and the Mappa Mundi, makes a good rainy-day trip too.
